title: Does School Spending Matter? The New Literature on an Old Question
research_question: Does increasing financial resources available to public schools improve student outcomes such as test scores, educational attainment, and later-life economic well-being? In particular, are the effects of additional school spending larger for children from low-income families, and do they differ across types of spending (e.g., general budget increases versus capital or targeted spending)?
data_description: The paper is a review synthesizing U.S.-based studies on school spending and student outcomes. It contrasts pre-1995 observational studies (summarized via the 163-study review by Hanushek 2003 and the Hedges et al. 1994 meta-analysis) with roughly 33 more recent quasi-experimental studies—13 multi-state/national and 20 single-state or single-city analyses. Outcome measures across the reviewed work include standardized test scores (e.g., NAEP and state assessments), high-school graduation, college enrollment and degree attainment, adult wages, poverty incidence, and intergenerational income mobility. Key inputs include district-level per-pupil expenditures, state aid formulas, local property tax revenues, and Title I allocations. Sample periods span from the early 1970s court-ordered reforms through post-2008 Great Recession years, with units of observation ranging from school districts and schools to student cohorts.
institutional_context: U.S. K-12 public schools are funded through a mix of local property taxes, state aid, and federal sources, producing large within-state spending disparities tied to neighborhood wealth. Beginning in 1971, state supreme courts in 28 states overturned existing finance systems, prompting school finance reforms that altered state aid formulas to compress spending gaps between wealthy and poor districts. Subsequent waves of reforms continued through 2010. Additional sources of funding variation reviewed include the Great Recession's asymmetric impact on states differentially reliant on state taxes for education, fluctuations in local property values feeding into fixed funding formulas, capital bond referenda, school construction programs, and the federal Title I program providing supplemental funds to high-poverty schools. These institutional features generate spending changes largely outside the control of individual families and local officials.
